title: How do climate scientists make predictions?
reason: 上一课聚焦日常口语焦虑，今天轮换到科技、数据与决策。本集用气候模型说明如何根据大量数据讨论不确定的未来，与企业级开发、平台工程和金融科技中常见的容量规划、风险评估及情景分析高度相关。练习反复调用表达条件、依赖、重要性、失衡和可选方案的高频词块，让学习者从理解模型逻辑逐步过渡到用简洁英语解释技术判断。

targetExpressions.meaning: produce conditional estimates of what may happen in different future situations
targetExpressions.usage: Use it for model-based future scenarios: The team uses traffic data to make projections for next quarter.

targetExpressions.meaning: be affected by additional conditions rather than being certain on its own
targetExpressions.usage: Name the result before the phrase: The final cost will depend on other factors.

targetExpressions.meaning: an informal pattern used to introduce the most important detail about something
targetExpressions.usage: Complete both parts of the pattern: The thing about forecasts is that they change when the inputs change.

targetExpressions.meaning: have an important influence on something
targetExpressions.usage: Follow it with a noun or -ing form: Reliable data plays a big part in good planning.

targetExpressions.meaning: out of balance or not working properly
targetExpressions.usage: Use it after be or get in informal English: The figures look out of whack after the failed import.

targetExpressions.meaning: not being considered as an option or possibility
targetExpressions.usage: Use it to rule out an option: Cancelling the security review is not on the table.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: Complete the contrast from the programme: Climate models do not make predictions; they ______.
objectiveQuestions.explanation: Kate Marvel says climate models make projections: conditional pictures of possible futures, rather than certain predictions.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: Why does the programme call a climate projection conditional?

options.text: Its result can depend on other factors, including human activity and emissions.
It reports one future that must happen in every situation.
It ignores physical and chemical data from around the world.
It measures temperature only in Fahrenheit.

objectiveQuestions.explanation: The transcript defines conditional as depending on other factors and identifies human activity, especially greenhouse gas emissions, as a main factor.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: Complete the pattern that introduces the key detail: “______ clouds is that they have a dual effect.”
objectiveQuestions.explanation: Kate uses “The thing about clouds is that...” to introduce the key fact that clouds can both cool and warm the planet.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: Which sentence best restates the programme's point about the importance of clouds?

options.text: Clouds play a big part in the climate because they can both block sunlight and trap heat.
Clouds play a big part the climate because they only make the planet colder.
Clouds play at a big part in climate models but have no effect on energy.
Clouds play a big part to remove the need for global data.

objectiveQuestions.explanation: The transcript says clouds play a big part in climate and explains their dual effect: blocking sunlight cools the planet, while their greenhouse effect warms it.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: Complete the programme's informal description: Scientists measure how much the Earth's energy balance is ______.
objectiveQuestions.explanation: The programme uses “out of whack” to describe an energy system that is out of balance or not working properly.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: What does Kate mean when she says “no climate change is unfortunately not on the table”?

options.text: Avoiding climate change completely is no longer an available option.
Scientists have decided not to discuss any climate models.
The climate problem has already been solved beyond doubt.
Only options written on a physical table can be considered.

objectiveQuestions.explanation: Phil explains that “not on the table” means not an option; here, a future with no climate change at all is not available.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: Complete the technical-planning sentence with today's expression: The release date may ______, such as test results and team capacity.
objectiveQuestions.explanation: “Depend on other factors” correctly shows that a projected result changes with additional conditions, just as climate projections do.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: Why are complex climate models necessary, according to the discussion?

options.text: They help scientists make projections so people can understand the direction of change and adapt.
They guarantee one exact temperature for every future year.
They prove clouds have only a cooling effect on the planet.
They replace the need for physical and chemical observations.

objectiveQuestions.explanation: The speakers say models turn large amounts of data into possible futures, and knowing the trajectory helps people prepare and adapt.

subjectiveQuestions.prompt: Write one sentence of 10–25 words. Why is a climate projection not certain? Start: “It is conditional because...” and use “depend on other factors”.
subjectiveQuestions.gradingCriteria: A supported answer should say that a projection is conditional because its result depends on factors such as human activity or emissions. First judge whether the content answers the question, then check whether “depend on other factors” is used naturally. Point out only one or two important improvements. Do not penalise simple but correct English for not being advanced. If useful, give only one alternative from today's target expressions or transcript. Distinguish missing meaning from correct meaning expressed less naturally.

subjectiveQuestions.gradingCriteria: A supported answer should explain that clouds play an important role because they cool the planet by blocking sunlight and warm it through their greenhouse effect. subjectiveQuestions.gradingCriteria: A successful answer should preserve the idea that completely avoiding climate change is not an available option while using “not on the table” naturally. First judge whether the meaning is preserved, then check the specified expression. Point out only one or two important improvements. Do not penalise simple but correct English for not being advanced. subjectiveQuestions.gradingCriteria: A successful answer should stay in the software-release scenario, give one future estimate, name two relevant conditions and naturally use at least one supplied phrase. First judge whether the content completes the task, then check expression use. Point out only one or two important improvements. Do not penalise simple but correct English for not being advanced. If useful, give only one alternative from today's target expressions or transcript. Distinguish missing meaning from correct meaning expressed less naturally.

subjectiveQuestions.gradingCriteria: A successful answer should give a clear view, one reason, one relevant example and use the full “the thing about... is...” pattern naturally. assessment.retellingPrompt: Without looking at the full transcript, retell the episode in 80–120 words using this structure: (1) method—how scientists use data and models; (2) two key ideas—the difference between predictions and projections, and the dual effect of clouds; (3) conclusion—why models still help people prepare and adapt. Phrase bank: “make projections”, “depend on other factors”, “out of whack”. Use at least two phrases naturally. Simple, accurate sentences are enough.
referencePoints: Scientists feed large amounts of physical and chemical data into supercomputers to model possible futures.
Climate models make conditional projections rather than certain predictions.
Human activity, especially greenhouse gas emissions, is a main factor affecting future climate outcomes.
Clouds have a dual effect: they cool the planet by blocking sunlight and warm it through their greenhouse effect.
Scientists measure the Earth's energy imbalance in Watts per square metre.
Models are complex but help people understand the trajectory, prepare and adapt; human-caused warming also means solutions are in human hands.
